Occurrences.Kwic: 萬年松拂日百怪石騰溪不一而一不二而二。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (L/L155/L155n1642.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Mingdao Zhengjue Sen (明道正覺森禪師語錄), words for sweeping the pagoda of the Tianmu ancestor. Speaker: Maoxi Xingsen, who says ‘not one yet one; not two yet two.’

Senses.Explanation: Not two is a predicate the records apply to named pairs. In the cited exchanges it does not end the inquiry: Foyan Qingyuan asks why ordinary people still drift while sages are free, and Yuanwu Keqin says that the phrase ‘not two’ has already made two. An unnamed monk quotes ‘only say not two’ and asks Fayan Wenyi what the words ‘not two’ are; Fayan replies, ‘Could you add a little more?’ Yuanwu Keqin is sharper: ‘As this mountain monk sees it, just this “not two” is already two.’ Zhongfeng Mingben calls Sengcan's wording both elixir and poison before citing Yuanwu's reply. Buyan Daole likewise says that an explanation of the inherited line has already become a sprawling mess; when he then asks ‘What is not two?’ he answers with Guanyin buying a rice cake and setting down a steamed bun. The phrase remains attached to explicit pairs. Huangbo Xiyun says speech is silence and silence is speech, then calls speech and silence not two. Foyan Qingyuan refuses to let recital settle the matter: if ordinary and holy are known as not two, why do ordinary people drift while sages are free; if delusion and awakening are known as not two, why is the deluded person still blocked while the awakened person remains alert? Tianyin Yuanxiu's verse similarly applies the words to death and life. At a Tianmu pagoda service, Maoxi Xingsen gives the compact counterpair ‘not one yet one; not two yet two.’

Occurrences.Kwic: 一時掃蕩總不要。是為入不二法門。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (T/T48/T48n2003.xml). Blue Cliff Record (佛果圜悟禪師碧巖錄): This is Yuanwu Keqin's prose comment after quoting Manjusri: he says the verbal positions are swept away all at once and calls that entering the gate of not-two.

Occurrences.Kwic: 第二諸菩薩各說入不二法門，以言顯於無言。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X83/X83n1578.xml). Record Pointing at the Moon (指月錄), Dazhu Huihai section: Dazhu Huihai speaks throughout the answer to a Vimalakirti lecturer; he distinguishes the chapter in which the bodhisattvas explain entry into not-two by using speech to display the speechless.

Senses.Explanation: The gate of not-two is the Vimalakirti case's challenge to meet what is 'not two' without freezing either speech or silence into the answer. Dazhu Huihai reads the case chapter by chapter: the bodhisattvas use speech to display the speechless, Manjusri uses the speechless to display the speechless, and Vimalakirti's silence gathers up the preceding words. Yuanwu Keqin likewise says the verbal positions are swept away all at once. The records refuse to leave the phrase as a settled label. An unnamed monk asks Dongshan Shouchu how to enter the gate and receives 'eyebrows three feet long'; an unnamed official asks Heyi Chaozi what it is and receives another concrete answer. Baiyan Fu says manifesting it would take three lives and sixty aeons. Zhongfeng Mingben can still call Pang's paired warnings a direct route into Vimalakirti's gate. Across these uses, the inherited case supplies the name, while masters turn it back into a question, an answer, an appraisal, and a warning against merely identifying it with muteness.

Senses.Explanation: Not obtained by seeking outside is a recurrent denial that the matter, precept-body, or responsive capacity must be acquired from elsewhere. Zhongfeng Mingben warns that merely repeating 'originally complete, requiring no outward search' can freeze inquiry before it has begun. Other speakers apply the formula affirmatively to the precept-body or to capacities said to be already complete. The warning is part of the entry's meaning: the phrase denies an external source but does not authorize verbal possession without investigation.

Senses.Explanation: The expression denies that the named object can be secured, found, or made available. Huike reports that, after searching for mind, he cannot obtain it; Dahui Zonggao applies the same denial to characteristics and emptiness, Chushi Fanqi to the present characteristic, and Wuyi Yuanlai to birth and death. Other cited speakers deny that knowledge, sight, or hearing can be obtained, fixing the literal range without making those ordinary objects a separate Chan sense.

Senses.Explanation: The proverb pictures someone unable to damage the boat taking the blow out on its bailer. Chan speakers use that displaced blow as a verdict on Nanquan breaking the cooking pot, on comments about Yangshan's hoe encounter, and on an inherited hall saying. Mingzhao Deqian adds the proverb after Nanquan breaks the pot; Jingqing Daofu uses it when asked about Xuansha's threat to kick over Yangshan's hoe; Po'an Zuxian turns it against Baoning's hall saying. Prefect Xu Shi says the same line after Letan and Shanglan exchange a shout, and Yingshan Zhiyin immediately raises it as the layman's verdict rather than claiming the words as his own.

Senses.Explanation: The phrase marks a doubt-producing remainder in a public appraisal. Youke Xuan and Huguo Yuan attach it to claims in raised cases; Natang Bian, Dahui Zonggao, and Baichi Xingyuan use it before exposing or resolving the particular point that still invites doubt. Youke Xuan says the demon king’s bold act could leave people doubtful, then criticizes his later promise; Huguo Yuan says the butcher’s laying down the knife would leave doubt until the added claim to be one of the thousand buddhas is examined; Natang Bian applies the phrase to the newborn Buddha before pointing to the proclamation that follows. Dahui Zonggao reports that Elder Qing’s treatment of Zhaozhou’s cypress answer can make people doubt before locating Qing’s claimed hinge; Baichi Xingyuan contrasts uncertainty before arrival with what becomes exposed upon arrival.

Senses.Explanation: The phrase commends a clean severance rather than further elaboration. Qiran and Yuanwu use it after pushing inquiry past remembered explanations, while Songyuan praises the same thoroughness in an old answer. Qiran Chaozhi says that careful inquiry may as well cut the matter off completely because what enters through the gate is not household treasure. Yuanwu Keqin follows the Mianzhou and Muzhou examples by saying that close examination cleanly ends talk of subtlety, principle, and rank. Songyuan Chongyue calls Suqi's answer—'a duck swallows a field snail'—thoroughly cut off.

Occurrences.Kwic: 不思量後，心歸何所？

ActorAttribution.GrammarEvidence: 都尉李公端愿問 names Li Zunxu as the questioner; 師云 introduces the master’s answer after this clause.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X79/X79n1557.xml). Linked Lamps Compendium: The lay official Li Zunxu asks where the mind returns after not deliberating; the master answers by sending the official home, making the negative condition part of a live exchange.

Senses.Explanation: Not deliberating negates the act of mentally considering a stated object or framing a response; the object and time-span must be recovered from its sentence. Dahui Zonggao recounts Mazu considering neither good nor evil, then says deliberation introduces coming and going. Elsewhere Dahui asks what it is when one neither distinguishes nor deliberates, making the negative condition itself part of a public question. Weilin Daopei twice raises Yaoshan’s wording: one address repeats the demand to consider what does not deliberate, and another asks how habitual deliberators could know it. Yun’e Xi specifies past affairs as the object and sets them beside anticipation of the future and lodging in the present. Guxue Zhe supplies the decisive limit: even neither deliberating nor framing an answer can still leave someone in the black-mountain ghost cave. Li Zunxu then asks where the mind goes after not deliberating and receives a situational answer, not a definition of blankness. The compound therefore does not by itself certify understanding or name blank mental absence.

Senses.Explanation: In the wild-fox case, 'not obscuring cause and effect' is Baizhang's turning answer; later comments question the fox's release and refuse to isolate it from the rejected companion phrase. The phrase is attested, almost exactly alongside 'not falling into cause and effect' (不落因果, 151); the paired form 'not falling, not being blind' (不落不昧) occurs 86 times. In the recorded Baizhang fox case, an old man asks whether a person of great conduct falls into cause and effect. Baizhang answers, 'not blind to cause and effect' (不昧因果), and the record says the old man was greatly awakened at the words and shed the fox body. Wansong Xingxiu explicitly contrasts the two phrases, while an unnamed monk inside the same commentary objects that even with 'not being blind to cause and effect' the fox body has not yet been shed. Dahui Zonggao preserves the paired questions but answers only by telling the questioner to raise them this way to people. Wumen Huikai asks why 'not falling' brought the fox body and why 'not being blind' shed it, then calls the pair 'two throws, one game' (不落不昧，兩采一賽). Chaozong Tongren rebukes both rejecting 'not falling' and clinging to 'not being blind' as tying oneself without a rope, yet continues by affirming 'not being blind to cause and effect' in his own stated frame. Later records continue asking whether the pair is the same or different. The records preserve competing uses and questions; this entry does not select a winner among them.

Senses.Explanation: ‘Do not understand’ (不會) denies comprehension. Baizhang Huaihai says that at a certain point he does not understand; the Prince of Zhending gives the same words as his entire answer to Zhaozhou Congshen; and Xinghua Cunjiang says that a visiting monk did not understand two gestures. Zhaozhou uses the negative in a conditional warning, while Gulin Qingmao and the Kangxi Emperor use it in verse questions. These differences of sentence and occasion do not change the thing denied: understanding.

Senses.Explanation: Not to be polluted is the condition articulated in the Nanyue Huairang–Huineng exchange about whether cultivation and verification are still needed. Nanyue says that cultivation and verification are not absent but pollution is not allowed; Huineng then calls this non-pollution what the buddhas protect. Later records preserve Huineng’s ratifying turn and Wuyi Yuanlai’s direct redeployment. The phrase is read with its paired cultivation clause, not as an isolated slogan.

Senses.Explanation: A transmission not based on written words, paired with direct pointing to the human mind rather than a ban on words, books, or scripture. Mi'an Xianjie recites the sequence of single transmission, not being based on written words, direct pointing to the human mind, and seeing one's nature. Yuanwu Keqin gives the Bodhidharma formula and then quotes Huineng's warning that even the words 'not establish' have already established something. Dahui Zonggao puts the formula into a question about why Bodhidharma spoke this way. Juelang Daosheng voices the apparent tension between the formula and Bodhidharma's use of the Descent into Lanka scripture as a seal. Guting Shanmi turns the slogan against itself by calling 'not established in written words' a world full of verbal vines and 'one's own contradiction.' These statements, questions, and criticisms all address the same formula; they do not establish separate senses.

Senses.Explanation: Not free names constraint: inability to move or respond readily, or an inward unease that does not let a person rest. Chan records trace it to deliberate contrivance and to carrying an asserted object “on the mind,” while a public case reverses the complaint by asking when one was ever not free. Miyun Yuanwu gives the clearest causal chain: deliberate contrivance leads to not being free, which prevents quick response and becomes obstruction. In a letter he also takes up a layman’s report of a subtle unease in the chest and analyzes four causes. Luohan Guichen turns the word into a public test. When Fayan locates a stone inside mind, Guichen asks how constrained a traveler becomes by carrying that stone on his mind. The record also preserves reversals and contrasts. Zhenjing Kewen answers “when were you ever not free?” after Huanglong Huinan challenges his claimed freedom, while Dahui describes circumstances in which neither the person’s own nor another person’s situation lacks freedom. The inward discomfort and restriction on response remain one state of constraint rather than different things. The corpus supplies no basis for turning the adjective into a named technical category or permanent human condition.

Senses.Explanation: Layman Pang’s fixed public question—who is not a companion of the ten thousand things?—is repeatedly raised afresh and answered in later records. Literally, not to be or become a companion to the myriad things. The expression is overwhelmingly recorded in the question, 'Who is the one who is not a companion to the myriad things?' The Compendium of the Five Lamps records Layman Pang asking it first of Shitou Xiqian, who covers Pang's mouth, and later of Mazu Daoyi, who answers, 'When you swallow the West River in one mouthful, I will tell you.' Later masters quote Pang's question as a named public case, ask it afresh, and give their own answers. Letan Huaicheng answers 'Guanyin' (觀世音菩薩). Caoshan Benji answers, 'Where did all those many people in Hongzhou city go?' (汝道洪州城裏如許多人甚麼處去). Asked directly, 'Ultimately, what is not being a companion to the myriad things?' (畢竟如何是不與萬法為侶), Yinyuan Longqi answers, 'Passing through a hundred flowers, not one leaf clings to the body' (百花叢裏過，一葉不沾身). Xingkong Zhen answers another fresh raising with 'standing openly revealed' (堂堂獨露). Yuanwu Keqin's instruction says that the ancients called someone 'the person who is not a companion to the myriad things' (古人謂之不與萬法為侶底人). Zhang Jun's preface to Yuanwu's record says that whenever Yuanwu raised this public case, it was already dragging through mud and water and falling into the second meaning. The entry preserves the fixed wording, its named origin, and the answers that the record attaches to it.

Senses.Explanation: Not falling into ranks denies placement on a graded ladder. The phrase enters questions about what remains when holy status, named stages, and even the claim of having no rank are put aside. Qingyuan asks Huineng what work does not fall into ranks and answers that even the holy truths are not undertaken. Jianfu answers with a wax person approaching fire; Ruiyan says there were never ranks to begin with; Furong speaks of a person who receives no imposed order.

Senses.Explanation: Do not recognize denies recognition of a person, object, or quality. Weilin Daopei says that living beings do not recognize the true mind and instead take up delusive thinking. Huangbo Xiyun says that Baizhang Huaihai's account lets him see Mazu Daoyi's great function and yet he does not recognize Mazu. Yongming Yanshou preserves a quoted blind-person analogy in which a person born blind does not recognize the color of milk. The sole supplementary lamp records Li Linzong giving a face-to-face answer to Yunfeng Yuanyi. Across these sources, the surrounding object supplies what is not recognized; the compound itself does not name a special state.

Senses.Explanation: The phrase faults someone for failing to distinguish black from white, and in these records it names failed discrimination in an encounter or in teaching. Xuansha Shibei joins it to 'not knowing auspicious from inauspicious' when rebuking students who only trade replies. Zhu'an Zhenyan applies it to hearers who hide in a formula about forms having no fixed character. A later record quotes Fenyang Shanzhao's stricter pairing, 'right and wrong not distinguished, black and white not divided,' as disqualification from judging for others.

Occurrences.Kwic: 故此一心法門。如鏡頓現。不待次第。如印頓成。更無前後。一見一切見。一聞一切聞。不俟推尋。若待了達而成。皆為權漸。若能觀於心性之一。則是一道甚深。即正道之一。是唯一之一。千佛同轍。今古不易之一道也。亦云一路涅槃門。亦云一道出生死。又名大佛頂首楞嚴王具足萬行。十方如來一門超出。妙莊嚴路。猶如百華共成一蜜。故知萬法同會斯宗。若諦了之。一切在我。昇沈去住。任意隨緣。示聖現凡。出生入死。變化難測。運無作之神通。隱顯同時。闡如幻之三昧。是非冥合。逆順同歸。語默卷舒。常順一真之道。治生產業。不違實相之門。運用施為。念念而未離法界。行住坐臥。步步而常在其中。若不信之人。對面千里。如寒山子詩云。可貴天然物。獨一無伴侶。促之在方寸。延之一切處。汝若不信受。相逢不相遇。如明達之者。寓目關懷。悉能先覺。若未遇之子。可以事知。舉動施為。未甞間斷。如蔡順。字君仲。以孝聞。順少孤。養母。常出求薪。有客卒至。母望順不還。乃嚙其指。順即心動。棄薪馳歸。跪問其故。母曰。有急客來。吾嚙指以悟汝耳。又唐裴敬彝。父為陳王典所殺。敬彝時在城。忽自覺。流涕不食。謂人曰。我大人凡有痛處。吾即不安。今日心痛。手足皆廢。事在不測。遂歸覲。父果已死。又唐張志安。居鄉閭稱孝。差為里尹。在縣忽稱母疾急。縣令問。志安曰。母有疾志安亦病。志安適患心痛。是以知母有疾。令拘之

Senses.Explanation: A thousand miles apart face-to-face describes separation despite immediate proximity. Yongming Yanshou applies it to a person who does not trust what is directly present; Yikui Yuankui joins it to hesitation; Guyin Yuncong contrasts those who know with those who remain far away. The retained capping verse makes even a hair of contrivance produce the same distance.

Senses.Explanation: To submit a failed showing is to be publicly charged with, or made to concede, a particular failure in an encounter or address. Zhanran Yuancheng refuses another failed showing after the proclamation; Juelang Daosheng contrasts exposing ancestral failures with submitting one; Xutang Zhiyu charges Shakyamuni with submitting one at death; and Yuanwu Keqin applies the phrase to a clumsy public display. The lay official Feng Ji directs the accusation at Dahui Zonggao, while a genuinely unnamed monk directs it at Xutang Zhiyu. Each verdict remains limited to the showing under review.

ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 土於億劫，贊皇圖於永年。誘引諸子，推排出火宅之門；拯拔迷流，踊躍登菩提之岸。且道畢竟從甚麼處建立？良久，云：拈出紅爐一點雪，長作人間六月冰。復舉：開元瑩禪師上堂語云：有一面鏡，到處懸掛。凡聖不來，誰上誰下？拈拄杖，云：這箇是拄杖，那箇是鏡？良久，云：萬古碧潭空界月，再三撈摝始應知。師云：歷劫無名，彰為古鏡。只要諸人知有，不為他影子所惑。瑩禪師大有為人處，山僧今日亦有一偈，不免舉似大眾：有一面鏡，到處懸掛。凡聖普現，非內非外。豎拂子，云：這箇是鏡，喚甚麼作拂子？還委悉麼？分明覿面別無真，休更迷頭猶認影。下座。多寶佛塔合尖陞座，師云：浮圖再造，多寶獨露全身；舍利斯藏，釋迦已分半座。壇場嚴淨，即是三變淨土；緇素雲集，何異十方分身？風鳴萬竅，如來親說法華；鳥噪千林，寶塔出聲讚善。古今一際，凡聖一源，體用一如，因果一法，靈山一會，儼然未散也。更看巍巍寶頂高踞七級之巔，燦燦金光遍照普天之下，直使有眼者見、有耳者聞、有心者知、有口者說，乃至童子嬉戲散心念佛，以及合郡官民紳士、男女老幼施食施財、搬磚運土，凡於此塔舉一念、捨一錢、用一力者，皆在如來授記之中，不特人天勝福而已。諸人還自信麼？良久，云：我不敢輕於汝等，汝等皆當作佛。下座。翠巖寺建殿陞梁示眾，師云：一毛端上，現寶王剎，百福莊嚴，普天歡洽。梁柱枋桷，主伴重重，共相成

ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 於長沙之鹿苑。當時衲子倔強如仰山者，猶下之而呼以為岑大蟲云。為之贊曰：長沙大蟲，聲威甚重，獨眠空林，百獸震恐。寂子兒癡，見不知畏，引手捋鬚，幾缺其耳。大空小空，是虎是你，如備與覺，可撩其尾。嗟今衲子，眼如裴旻，但見其彪，安識虎真？我拜公像，非存非沒，百尺竿頭，行塵勃勃。白雲端禪師曰：天下叢林之興，大智禪師力也。祖堂當設達磨初祖之像於其中，大智禪師像西向，開山尊宿像東向，得其宜也。不當止設開山尊宿，而略其祖宗耳。雲居祐禪師曰：吾觀諸方長老示滅，必塔其骸。山川有限，而人死無窮，百千年之下，塔將無所容。於是於宏覺塔之東作卵塔，曰：凡住持者，自非生身不壞，火浴雨舍利者，皆以骨石填於此。其西又作卵塔，曰：凡眾僧化，皆藏骨石於此。謂之三塔。二大老識度高遠，可為後世法。然孤論難持，犯眾難成，卒必有賞音者，吾將觀焉。東京覺嚴寺有誠法師，講華嚴經，歷席最久，學者依以揚聲。其為人純至，少緣飾，高行遠識，近世講人，莫有居其右者。元祐初，高麗僧統航海至，上表乞傳持賢首宗教，歸本國流通。奉聖旨下兩街，舉可以授法者。有司以師為宜，上表辭免曰：臣雖刻意講學，識趣淺陋，特以年運已往，妄為學者所推。今異國名僧，航海問道，宜得高識博聞者為之師。竊見杭州慧因院僧道源，精練教乘，旁通外學，舉以自代，實允公議。奉聖旨依所乞，勑差朝奉郎揚傑館伴，至錢

Senses.Explanation: A slow or incapable bird settling in reeds is an image of stopping at a dependent resting place. Jiashan Shanhui pairs it with a stranded fish while refusing dependence on cloud-and-water wandering. Tianyi Zai applies it to Vimalakirti’s silence; Shengke Deyu uses it for beings still to be delivered, and Xisou Shaotan for the fixed confinement of the summer retreat.
